result: The study demonstrates that successive relays in the parasympathetic nervous system (preganglionic to ganglion and postganglionic to gland) exhibit remarkably similar organizational principles and developmental strategies. Both levels show single innervation of targets via basket-like endings that emerge through postnatal synaptic pruning and elaboration, despite different embryological origins of the cells involved.
evaluation: Claims C2, C3, C56, C57, C59, C60 provide converging anatomical and developmental evidence from both light and electron microscopy showing parallel organization at both synaptic relays. The data demonstrate single innervation (C56), basket formation (C57), developmental transition from multiple to single innervation (C59), and postnatal pruning (C60) at both levels. Claims C61 and C91 appropriately synthesize these findings into a coherent conclusion about the fundamental role of synapse elimination in establishing this organization.

result: Adult parasympathetic postganglionic axons form basket-like terminal structures that are localized to intercalated duct-acinar cell assemblies, with each assembly innervated by only one axon. Individual axons elaborate approximately 14 baskets confined to ~1% of the gland area, and these baskets from different axons segregate into non-overlapping territories.
evaluation: Claims C15, C17, C19 provide direct observational evidence from fluorescent labeling and Brainbow experiments showing basket structures and their segregation. Claims C18, C20 provide inference supported by high transfection efficiency (>80%) showing lack of overlap. Claims C26, C27 provide quantitative measurements (n=4 axons) of basket distribution and number. The convergence of multiple imaging approaches (transgenic labeling, Brainbow, confocal microscopy) strongly supports these anatomical findings.

result: Electron microscopy reconstruction reveals that the salivary gland parenchyma contains three major cell types (acinar cells, intercalated duct cells, and myoepithelial cells), and that a single axon innervates all three cell types within a reconstructed region with synapses distributed as ~25% on duct cells, ~73% on myoepithelial cells, and ~2% on acinar cells.
evaluation: Claim C21 provides detailed EM characterization of cell types. Claims C23 and C24 provide quantitative synapse counts from EM reconstruction showing single axon innervation of multiple cell types. Claim C25 adds the observation that axons don't contact each other, ruling out contact-mediated mechanisms. The EM data provides high-resolution structural validation of the light microscopy findings, though the sample size is limited to one reconstructed volume.

result: Postganglionic axon arbors undergo developmental refinement during the first three postnatal weeks. While absolute arbor size remains relatively constant, the gland grows substantially, resulting in axons occupying progressively smaller proportions of the gland. Concurrently, axons transition from unbranched termini at P1 to elaborate basket structures by P21, with a decrease in non-basket terminals and increase in basket terminals, accompanied by increased branching complexity and decreased arbor overlap.
evaluation: Claims C28-C30 provide statistical comparisons with appropriate tests, sample sizes (N=17), confidence intervals, and p-values showing the relationship between arbor size, gland size, and normalized arbor size. Claim C31 appropriately interprets the normalized data. Claims C32-C36 provide quantitative developmental data on terminal morphology, branch order, and overlap. The statistical analyses appear appropriate for the data, though the conclusion about pruning (C31) is inferential. The convergence of multiple quantitative measures supports the developmental refinement model.

result: Early postnatal development (P3) shows extensive overlap of multiple postganglionic axons innervating the same intercalated duct-acinar cell assemblies, with multiple axons containing synaptic vesicles in close proximity to the same targets. By P7, basket terminals show no intermixing, indicating that synapse elimination occurs during early postnatal life to establish single innervation.
evaluation: Claims C37 and C38 provide direct observational evidence from multicolor labeling at P3 and P7 showing the developmental transition. Claims C39 and C40 provide EM validation of multiple axons with vesicles near the same assembly at P3. Claims C41 and C42 appropriately infer synapse elimination from the developmental transition. The combination of light microscopy (showing overlap changes) and EM (showing multiple axons with vesicles) provides strong converging evidence for the synapse elimination mechanism.

result: Adult preganglionic axons establish multiple basket endings on sporadically distributed ganglion cells (approximately 25 baskets per axon), with each basket representing the dominant synaptic input to an individual adendritic ganglion cell. Preganglionic axons also possess occasional unbranched terminals that may correspond to weak secondary inputs observed electrophysiologically.
evaluation: Claims C44, C46, C47 provide direct anatomical observations from reconstructed preganglionic axons showing basket distribution patterns. Claim C45 provides cited support for the adendritic nature of adult ganglion cells. Claim C48 documents the presence of non-basket terminals. Claim C49 appropriately connects anatomical observations to prior electrophysiological data. The anatomical findings are consistent with established electrophysiological knowledge (C43, C45), providing convergent validation. Sample size is limited (n=3 reconstructed axons mentioned).

result: At P3, preganglionic axons are more highly branched than in adults and lack basket-shaped terminals. EM reconstruction of two adjacent P3 ganglion cells shows they possess multiple dendrites and are innervated by 14 and 17 separate axonal branches, respectively. Computational analysis of branch sampling suggests these likely represent 7-17 different preganglionic axons per ganglion cell.
evaluation: Claims C50 and C51 provide direct observations from fluorescent labeling of P3 preganglionic axons. Claims C52 and C53 provide EM data showing multiple dendrites and innervating branches. Claims C54 and C55 provide computational validation using random volume sampling (10,000 iterations) to estimate the probability that branches belong to the same axon. The computational approach is creative and appropriate for addressing the limitation that individual axons cannot be distinguished in EM. The convergence of light microscopy morphology and EM branch counts with statistical validation supports the conclusion of multiple innervation at P3.

result: The demonstration of synapse elimination in salivary glands represents only the second known site (after skeletal muscle) where axonal reorganization occurs in non-neuronal targets. Importantly, gland target cells do not fire action potentials and use metabotropic receptors, indicating that axon pruning can occur without sodium-based postsynaptic action potential activity.
evaluation: Claim C62 appropriately contextualizes the novelty of the finding based on field knowledge and the current data. Claims C63-C65 provide cited support for the properties of different target cells and prior experimental manipulations. Claim C66 appropriately infers from the current findings that action potentials are not required for synapse elimination. The logic is sound: if synapse elimination occurs in glands (demonstrated in this study) and gland cells don't fire action potentials (C63), then action potentials are not required. This challenges previous assumptions about mechanisms of synapse elimination.

result: The anatomical organization suggests a 'neuro-lobular' functional unit where a single preganglionic axon drives a cohort of synchronously active ganglion cells, which in turn innervate neighboring regions of the gland. This arrangement may allow a single brainstem neuron to produce sufficient coordinated salivary secretion to overcome ductal compliance and reach the oral cavity.
evaluation: Claim C71 is supported by anatomical data (Figure 9A). Claim C72 infers synchronous activity from cited electrophysiology showing single dominant inputs. Claims C73-C75 build a logical functional model from the anatomical organization. However, this functional interpretation is largely speculative (C75 explicitly notes this). No direct physiological measurements of coordinated secretion or ductal compliance are provided. The anatomical organization is well-documented, but the functional consequences require experimental validation. The analogy to motor units (C76-C77) supports plausibility but doesn't constitute direct evidence.

result: The study proposes that synapse elimination must occur in a peripheral-to-central sequence (gland before ganglion) based on activity-dependent competition mechanisms. If ganglion cells became singly innervated first, synchronously active ganglion cells would innervate the same gland targets, preventing activity-dependent elimination. Evidence consistent with this includes earlier basket formation in glands and later completion of synapse elimination in ganglia (~P30).
evaluation: Claims C79 and C82 provide cited support for activity-dependent synapse elimination principles. Claims C80 and C81 present a logical argument for the required sequence based on these principles. The logic is internally consistent: synchronous inputs don't compete (C82), so gland elimination must precede ganglionic elimination to maintain asynchrony. However, claims C83 and C84 provide only limited supporting evidence - C83 is preliminary data and C84 shows timing differences but doesn't directly demonstrate the proposed mechanism. The argument is compelling but requires more direct experimental validation of the activity patterns and their causal role in the proposed sequence.

result: The authors propose an evolutionary interpretation where peripheral-to-central maturation allows the nervous system to adapt to evolutionary changes in peripheral structures. This is supported by evidence that the nervous system evolves more slowly than other organ systems and by classic experiments showing nervous system adaptation to altered peripheral structures.
evaluation: Claims C85-C87 provide cited support for established principles about neurotrophic regulation and evolutionary rates. Claim C89 cites classic experiments showing nervous system plasticity. However, claims C88 and C90 are explicitly speculative interpretations applying these principles to the current findings. While the evolutionary argument is plausible and draws on established principles, it lacks direct experimental support. The connection between the observed developmental sequence and evolutionary adaptation is inferential. This represents an interesting hypothesis that would require comparative studies across species or experimental manipulations to validate.

result: The study discusses potential mechanisms for synapse elimination in glands, suggesting that calcium signaling in myoepithelial cells, potentially propagated through electrical junctions, could mediate competitive synapse loss across the entire intercalated duct-acinar cell assembly, contrasting with the electrically isolated muscle fibers during neuromuscular synapse elimination.
evaluation: Claim C67 provides cited support for calcium-dependent competition in cerebellar climbing fibers. Claims C68 and C70 provide cited evidence for calcium surges in myoepithelial cells and electrical junctions. However, claim C69 is explicitly speculative about the mechanism in glands. No direct measurements of calcium dynamics, electrical coupling during synapse elimination, or causal manipulations are provided. The hypothesis is plausible given the cited properties of myoepithelial cells, but remains untested. This represents a mechanistic proposal that requires future experimental validation.

result: Sympathetic postganglionic axons exhibit sparse terminal arbors with homogeneously distributed varicosities, contrasting with the basket-like parasympathetic terminals.
evaluation: Claim C16 is directly observed in Thy1 YFP16 mice and shown in Figure 1D. This provides a useful anatomical contrast to highlight the distinctive organization of parasympathetic innervation. The observation is straightforward and well-documented.

result: Electrical junctions exist between acinar cells, duct cells, and myoepithelial cells, suggesting the intercalated duct-acinar cell assembly may operate as a functional unit.
evaluation: Claim C22 is supported by citations to previous studies (Ihara et al., 2000; Kater and Galvin, 1978) demonstrating electrical junctions. The inference that this creates a functional unit is reasonable given the electrical coupling, though direct functional measurements in the context of neural activation are not provided in this study.

result: The introduction establishes the context of synaptic reorganization in neural development, reviews prior work on synapse elimination in various systems including the visual system, cerebellum, and neuromuscular junction, and describes established knowledge about the submandibular ganglion system.
evaluation: These claims provide appropriate background context supported by citations to established literature (C4-C8, C11) and general neuroscience knowledge (C1, C6, C9, C12, C14). Claim C10 appropriately identifies a gap in knowledge. Claim C13 cites the authors' previous work. These claims establish the scientific context and rationale for the current study.

result: Prior electrophysiological studies established that adult submandibular ganglion cells are typically singly innervated following developmental synapse elimination.
evaluation: Claim C43 appropriately cites previous electrophysiological work (Lichtman, 1977) that established single innervation of adult ganglion cells. This provides important context for interpreting the anatomical findings in the current study.

result: The study draws an analogy to motor units in skeletal muscle, where localized activation is more effective than distributed activation due to overcoming visco-elastic properties, and suggests that without synapse elimination, gland innervation would be weak and distributed rather than strong and focused.
evaluation: Claim C76 is supported by citation to previous work on motor unit organization. Claim C77 represents established knowledge of muscle physiology. Claim C78 is a logical counterfactual argument about the consequences of no synapse elimination. These claims provide useful functional context through analogy, though they don't constitute direct experimental evidence for the gland system.
